short_title: National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC
full_title: NATIONAL PRESS CLUB OF THE PHILIPPINES, AUTOMATED ELECTION SYSTEM WATCH, AND GUARDIANS BROTHERHOOD, INC., PETITIONERS, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, RESPONDENT.

doctrine:
**Ballot printing.** Under **Section 187 of the Omnibus Election Code**, upon the request of any candidate, political party, or civic, religious, professional, business, service, youth or similar organization collectively designated by the COMELEC, the COMELEC "shall" allow the designated watchers to witness the printing and distribution of ballots and returns and to guard the printer's premises. **This is a ministerial duty that mandamus can compel.** Security zones, schedule pressures and pandemic health protocols do not excuse a refusal. The COMELEC may limit the number of watchers or use other means such as livestreaming, "[t]his is not to say, however, that on-site viewing of the printing process may be dispensed with entirely."

**AES equipment.** Under **Section 14 of RA 8436, as amended by RA 9369**, the COMELEC has no discretion to refuse political parties, candidates, citizens' arms or their representatives the right to **examine and test** the equipment or devices of the AES. This covers not only the vote-counting machines but other devices such as **SD cards**, "even up to the day of the electoral exercise, before voting starts." The right does not depend on compliance with COMELEC guidelines (reiterating *Bagumbayan-VNP*), but the COMELEC may first verify that the requester is a bona fide party, candidate, citizens' arm or authorized representative. **The law does not require the COMELEC to allow witnessing of the configuration and preparation of SD cards and VCMs**; testing presupposes configured devices. On **digital signatures**, the COMELEC's choice to have only electoral boards in highly urbanized cities digitally sign the returns is discretionary and not compellable by mandamus. The VCM's own digital signature is the functional equivalent required by Section 22 of the AES Law.

**Right to information.** The transmission diagram and data/communications network architecture of the VCMs are matters of public concern. Exemptions are construed strictly against confidentiality, and the agency bears the burden of proving an exemption. **Absent mootness, the COMELEC could be compelled by mandamus to disclose them**, but not a vague demand for "all details" of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room" that could compromise security. The right to information does **not** include **physical access** to the COMELEC's hubs, servers and data centers, which Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes "whether classified or declassified." A citizen invoking the right to information has standing to seek mandamus (reiterated). The Court resolved these issues despite mootness because the case involved paramount public interest, required controlling principles, and was capable of repetition yet evading review.
facts:
About 48 days before the May 2022 National and Local Elections (NLE), and 18 days before overseas voting began, petitioners National Press Club of the Philippines, AES Watch, and Guardians Brotherhood, Inc. filed a petition for mandamus with the Supreme Court. They sought to compel the COMELEC to (a) implement the use of digital signatures, and (b) allow political parties, candidates, media and other organizations to access and inspect the "Election Transparency Activities." These were: the printing of ballots at the National Printing Office (NPO); the disposition of some 5.2 million defective ballots; the configuration of SD cards at the Sta. Rosa, Laguna warehouse and the Pre-Logic and Accuracy Test; the preparation and testing of VCMs; the technical support center, hubs and data centers; and the transmission diagram or network architecture, including the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room."

The COMELEC had approved digital signatures in Minute Resolution No. 210021 (January 20, 2021). At the March 9, 2022 Joint Congressional Oversight Committee (JCOC) hearing, however, it was revealed that only electoral boards in the NCR, Cebu City and Davao City would digitally sign. Commissioner Casquejo's March 7, 2022 letter explained that no provider could supply enough cable assemblies for the approximately 300,000 to 350,000 teachers. Political parties had asked in writing, as early as January 2022, to observe the ballot printing. The COMELEC refused, citing restricted security areas at the NPO, possible delays in preparing for overseas voting starting April 10, 2022, and COVID-19 limits on persons in the premises. By the March 9, 2022 hearing, 66.4% of the ballots had been printed without witnesses. Party representatives also testified that they were turned away at the Sta. Rosa warehouse where SD cards were configured, though without any formal denial.

After the hearing, Commissioner Casquejo apologized and said the pandemic was no excuse to bar observers. The COMELEC began livestreaming the printing on March 17, 2022, offered CCTV footage for the earlier period, and conducted random ballot checking with stakeholders. It invited the public to the final testing and sealing of VCMs on May 2–7, 2022 and opened the Sta. Rosa warehouse to public viewing. It also posted its local hubs and dispatch schedules (March 16, 2022), held an end-to-end AES demonstration (March 22, 2022) and a Transparency Media Server walkthrough (April 30, 2022), and disclosed the locations of its data centers. In its July 14, 2022 Comment, the COMELEC argued that the petition was moot after the elections, that it had not neglected any duty, that the law did not require access to SD card configuration or its hubs and data centers, and that the issues were political questions.
issues: Whether the petition should be dismissed as moot, and whether the Court should nonetheless resolve the issues.
Whether petitioners have legal standing to file the petition for mandamus.
Whether mandamus lies to compel the COMELEC to implement the use of digital signatures nationwide.
Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to allow watchers to witness the printing of ballots.
Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to allow the witnessing of the configuration and preparation of SD cards and VCMs, or their examination and testing.
Whether the COMELEC may be compelled to disclose the transmission diagram, the data/communications network architecture, and all details of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room."
Whether the COMELEC has a ministerial duty to allow physical access to its technical hubs, servers and data centers.
ruling:
**1. The petition is moot, but the Court ruled on the issues.** With the 2022 NLE over, no relief could be granted. But three exceptions to mootness were present: the exceptional character of the situation and paramount public interest, the need to formulate controlling principles, and the case being capable of repetition yet evading review. The case presented "novel issues" on the COMELEC's duties regarding SD cards, VCMs, and its hubs, servers and data centers.

**2. Yes, petitioners have standing.** Under *Guingona v. COMELEC*, a mandamus petition anchored on the right to information may be filed by any citizen without showing a special interest. Petitioners' members are registered voters, journalists and concerned citizens. AES Watch's signatory, however, lacked proof of authority to sign the verification and certification against forum shopping. The Court restated the five requisites of mandamus: a clear legal right, a duty mandated by law, unlawful neglect, a ministerial (not discretionary) act, and no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy.

**3. No, mandamus does not lie for digital signatures.** The first paragraph of Section 22 of RA 8436, as amended, which requires signing and thumbmarking, refers to printed election returns. Digital signatures appear only on electronic returns. Since 2010, the digital signatures on returns have come from the machines, and under *Capalla* and *Bagumbayan-VNP* a machine signature is the functional equivalent of a digital signature. How to digitally sign results is subject to the COMELEC's sound judgment (*AES Watch v. COMELEC*), and courts will not interfere with its choice of means unless clearly illegal or a gross abuse of discretion (*Sumulong*). **The VCM-generated signatures outside HUCs were sufficient compliance; "[t]he job of the Court is to say what the law is, not to dictate how another branch, agency, or instrumentality of government should do its job."**

**4. Yes, but the issue is moot.** **By the word "shall" in Section 187 of the OEC, the COMELEC has no discretion. Once a qualified requester designates watchers, allowing them to witness the printing is a ministerial duty.** The COMELEC's reasons failed. Restricted areas did not matter because watchers may even guard the printer's premises. The overseas-voting delay was a "flimsy excuse" given requests made as early as January 2022. Health protocols "did not authorize the COMELEC to disregard the law"; it could have allowed limited watchers or used other methods. The law does not limit the means, and livestreaming strikes a balance, though on-site viewing may not be dispensed with entirely. The COMELEC's later livestreaming, CCTV access and random checks made the issue moot.

**5. Witnessing of configuration, no; examination and testing, yes, but the issue is moot.** RA 9369 replaced "counting machines" with "equipment or device of the AES." Congress thus expanded examination and testing beyond VCMs to devices such as SD cards. **But the law requires only examination and testing, not access to configuration and preparation.** Because the COMELEC must provide test ballots and test forms, testing takes place after configuration; "it would be absurd to allow the examination and testing of unconfigured equipment or devices." Petitioners also failed to prove that watchers of the requesting parties were denied entry to Sta. Rosa or that the lawyers turned away represented any party, candidate or citizens' arm. The right to examine and test does not depend on COMELEC guidelines, but the COMELEC may verify that the requester is a bona fide party, candidate, accredited citizens' arm or authorized representative, since an "unscrupulous individual could feign examination and testing in order to compromise the equipment." The May 2–7, 2022 public testing and sealing and the opening of the Sta. Rosa warehouse made the issue moot.

**6. The transmission diagram, yes; "all details," no; the issue is moot.** RA 9369 protects the secrecy and sanctity of "all election, consolidation and transmission documents" "in order that the process shall be transparent and credible" and elections "informed." Transparency matters more in an AES, which is "inherently less transparent" than manual counting; "the credibility of the system is directly proportional to the transparency of the entire process." Mandamus to enforce the right to information requires (a) a matter of public concern and (b) no exemption by law. Exemptions are construed against confidentiality, and the agency bears the burden of proving one. **The COMELEC failed to discharge that burden as to the transmission diagram and network architecture of the VCMs, so "were it not for the mootness of the issue," it could be compelled to disclose them.** The request for "all details" of the transmission router server and "Meet-Me Room" was "too vague and broad." Mandamus will not compel disclosure "for the sake of transparency but at the expense of the security, integrity, and credibility of the AES." Coverage of such documents should be decided case by case, not by a "shotgun approach."

**7. No.** The law does not require the COMELEC to allow physical access to its hubs, servers and data centers. **The right to information does not extend to physical access to facilities.** Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes "[g]aining or causing access to . . . facilities . . . whether classified or declassified," regardless of authorization. At most, the COMELEC may be compelled to provide information on its hubs and data centers, as it already had. Unlike the watchers' right at the printer's premises, there is no clear legal right to physical access.
disposition: The Petition was DISMISSED for being moot and academic.

bar_questions.q: Two months before a national election, Partido Bago, an accredited political party, wrote the COMELEC asking that its designated watchers be allowed to witness the printing of official ballots at the printing plant. The COMELEC denied the request, citing (1) security-restricted areas inside the plant, (2) the risk of delaying the printing of overseas ballots, and (3) health protocols limiting the number of persons inside. Partido Bago files a petition for mandamus. Will mandamus lie?

alac.answer: Yes. Allowing the designated watchers to witness the printing of ballots is a ministerial duty of the COMELEC, and its reasons do not justify the refusal.
alac.legal_basis: Section 187 of the Omnibus Election Code provides that, upon the request of any candidate, political party or organization collectively designated by the COMELEC, the COMELEC "shall" allow its designated watchers to witness the printing and distribution of ballots and returns and to guard the premises of the printer. By the word "shall," the COMELEC has no discretion. Once a request is made and watchers are designated, allowing them to observe the printing is ministerial and may be compelled by mandamus. (National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc)
alac.application: Partido Bago made a written request and designated watchers, so the COMELEC's duty arose. Restricted areas are no excuse, because the law even allows watchers to guard the printer's premises. Possible delay is a weak excuse where the request was made well ahead of time. Health protocols do not authorize the COMELEC to disregard the law: it could allow a limited number of watchers or use other means such as livestreaming, though on-site viewing cannot be dispensed with entirely. The COMELEC refused outright instead.
alac.conclusion: Mandamus will lie to compel the COMELEC to allow Partido Bago's designated watchers to witness the printing of the ballots.

bar_questions.q: Before an automated election, Bantay Halalan, an accredited citizens' arm, demanded that the COMELEC allow its representatives (a) to watch the configuration and loading of contents into the SD cards at the COMELEC warehouse, and (b) to enter the central data center housing the transmission router and inspect the servers. The COMELEC refused both demands but offered to let Bantay Halalan examine and test the configured VCMs and SD cards up to election day, before voting starts. May the COMELEC be compelled by mandamus to grant demands (a) and (b)?

alac.answer: (a) No. The law does not require the COMELEC to allow witnessing of the configuration of SD cards. (b) No. There is no right to physical access to the COMELEC's data centers.
alac.legal_basis: Section 14 of RA 8436, as amended by RA 9369, requires the COMELEC to allow political parties, candidates, citizens' arms or their representatives to examine and test the equipment or devices of the AES, including SD cards, even up to the day of the electoral exercise, before voting starts. It does not require access to the configuration and preparation of those devices; testing presupposes configured devices. The right to information does not extend to physical access to the COMELEC's hubs, servers and data centers, and Section 35(c) of RA 8436, as amended, penalizes gaining or causing access to such facilities whether classified or declassified. (National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc)
alac.application: (a) The COMELEC's offer to let Bantay Halalan examine and test the configured VCMs and SD cards is exactly what the law requires. Watching the configuration itself is not a duty the law imposes, so there is no ministerial duty to compel. (b) No law grants a right to enter the data center, and entry would fall within the acts Section 35(c) penalizes. At most, the COMELEC may be compelled to provide information about its data centers, not physical access.
alac.conclusion: Mandamus will not issue for either demand, although Bantay Halalan is entitled to examine and test the configured equipment and devices.

bar_questions.q: A group of journalists and registered voters asked the COMELEC for copies of the transmission diagram and data/communications network architecture of the vote-counting machines for the coming elections. They also asked for "all details of all devices and equipment used to transmit election results." The COMELEC refused both requests, stating only that the documents are "sensitive." The group files a petition for mandamus. (a) Does the group have standing? (b) Will mandamus lie as to each request?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, the group has standing as citizens. (b) Mandamus will lie to compel disclosure of the transmission diagram and network architecture, but not the vague request for "all details" of the transmission devices.
alac.legal_basis: When a petition for mandamus is anchored on the right to information on matters of public concern (Const., Art. III, Sec. 7; Art. II, Sec. 28), any citizen is a real party-in-interest without need of a special interest. Mandamus may compel disclosure when the information is of public concern and not exempt by law. Every claim of exemption is construed liberally in favor of disclosure and strictly against confidentiality, must be clearly asserted with its grounds, and must be proved by the agency. In National Press Club of the Philippines v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 259354, June 13, 2023, En Banc), the Court held that the transmission diagram and network architecture of the VCMs are matters of public concern that the COMELEC could be compelled to disclose. It also held that a prayer for "all details" of the transmission router server is too vague and broad, and that disclosure cannot be compelled at the expense of the security, integrity and credibility of the AES.
alac.application: (a) The members are journalists and registered voters asserting the people's right to information, so they need not show a personal stake. (b) The transmission diagram and network architecture bear directly on the integrity of election results, which is a matter of public concern. Calling them "sensitive," without specifying a legal ground for exemption, does not discharge the COMELEC's burden, so disclosure may be compelled. The demand for "all details of all devices and equipment" is too broad to identify what must be disclosed and could expose confidential security information, so mandamus will not lie for it.
alac.conclusion: The group has standing and may compel disclosure of the transmission diagram and network architecture, but not of "all details" of the transmission devices.

notes: The fallo only dismisses the petition as moot; the rulings on the COMELEC's duties were made under the exceptions to mootness. Votes: Leonen, SAJ. (Acting C.J.) concurred with a separate opinion disagreeing on SD card configuration and access to hubs; Caguioa, J. wrote a separate concurring opinion; Lazaro-Javier, J. concurred. These separate opinions are not examinable and were not used. Several post-filing COMELEC measures (livestreaming from March 17, 2022, public testing and sealing on May 2–7, 2022, opening of the Sta. Rosa warehouse) are taken from the Court's judicial notice of media reports. The 2027 syllabus has no specific Election Law heading on the automated election system; the COMELEC powers heading is the closest.
